entries.title: A History of the Novel in Britain by Philip Hensher review – a masterpiece of criticism

entries.content:
In his opening paragraph, Philip Hensher declares that a novel not only “tells a good story” but is a good story in itself. We could extend that neat formula to include this book, which is not only a masterful account of fiction since 1719, when Daniel Defoe set Robinson Crusoe down on his desert island, but is itself a wonderful read. There is nothing dreary here; no sense of being back in the seminar room taking notes. Instead it is 600 pages of deep pleasure, an excuse to revisit old literary loves and be reminded of ones that have slipped from view.

Hensher is smart enough to know why his book works so well and vain enough to tell us. The usual methodology for a survey is to assemble a roster of academics and invite them to trot out a chapter on their specialism, whether that be “Thomas Hardy” or “High Modernism”. The result is a series of silos, with little sense of historical connection or intellectual unfolding. Hensher, by contrast, gives us a joined-up account of creative call and response. Equally crucial to this project’s success is Hensher’s own experience as a novelist. He brings a practitioner’s informed eye to such questions as why some chapters in Dickens’s Dombey and Son are in the present tense or how Henry James pulls off free indirect speech in What Maisie Knew.

After setting out the novel’s origin story, we are plunged into the inky churn of the middle-18th century. Samuel Richardson writes Pamela in 1740, Henry Fielding shoots back with his snarky parody, Shamela (1741), followed by the more sustained inversion of Joseph Andrews (1742). Richardson, in turn infuriated by the lack of moral purpose in Fielding’s Tom Jones (1749), storms back with The History of Sir Charles Grandison (1754).

Hensher is brilliant on the warring duo’s finances, giving us a forensic account of the risk and reward of their different publishing models. Richardson was a printer before he was an author and hung on to his own copyrights. This allowed him the autonomy to shape the fledgling genre in ways that he wanted which, in the case of Clarissa (1748), meant 1m words written entirely in epistolary form. Fielding, no less lucky, had a patron and printer who supported him no matter how eccentric his artistic choices.

Few authors were so favoured. Jane Austen chose to sell Pride and Prejudice for a flat fee to Thomas Egerton in 1812, having previously lost money on Sense and Sensibility when she insisted on retaining copyright and paying for the printing. Under the new arrangement, Egerton was under no obligation to spend more than the minimum on production. When Pride and Prejudice eventually appeared in 1813 it was in such tiny print and scrappy paper that disgruntled readers decreed it “almost unintelligible”.

That sort of thing can kill a career, but Austen went on to rise above it, even if it took until the 1940s before the literary establishment caught up with her glory. One of the delights of Hensher’s capacious narrative is being alerted to authors and books that never got their proper due. Hannah More, usually written off as a Sunday school prig, turns out to be “a beautiful and graceful writer”, while Tobias Smollett, who generally gets dismissed these days as an unfunny hack, is rehabilitated as an inventive craftsman with supreme control over narrative voice. Arnold Bennett, characterised as a dreary bore thanks to Virginia Woolf’s unkind take-down of 1924, is lovingly restored as the author of the incomparable Old Wives Tale (1908), which “ought to be acknowledged among the 20 greatest novels in English”.

If Hensher is generous with plaudits, he is equally vigorous in his loathing. Ann Radcliffe, author of the hugely popular and preposterously gothic The Mysteries of Udolpho (1794) “was (and remains) a simply terrible writer”. DM Thomas, Booker nominated in 1981 for The White Hotel, is “patently untalented”. And poor David Lodge, who tried so hard with modish literary pastiche in Changing Places (1975), is simply “not up to the task”.

Hensher never falls into crankiness, but he is unafraid to point out home truths. Such as the fact that so much of the pleased-with-itself “experimentalism” of the 1960 to 1980 period was merely a retread of things that had been done better before. Tickled by the clever wheeze of having central characters with no name? Fanny Burney was already doing that in 1814. Keen on using fragmentary collage to signal modernity? That blustery old fogey Evelyn Waugh got their first with Vile Bodies (1930). As for self-reflexivity, that process by which the novelist comments on the process of writing a novel, you should go back to Fielding.

Hensher doesn’t bring his account right up to date, preferring to stop in 2000 – at Zadie Smith and her “wonderful ear for speech” – on the grounds that it is impossible to form a proper critical judgment until plenty of time has passed. It is a wise decision and a tactful one, underscoring the moral seriousness of this master­piece, quite aside from its buoyant joy. Reader, I could not put it down.

entries.title: Feel the burn: why holidays from hell make for blistering fiction
entries.summary: Family fallouts, failing marriages, sunburn, food poisoning ... from Deborah Levy’s hypnotic and disturbing Hot Milk to All In, Claire Powell’s all-inclusive nightmare, Leon Craig looks at the best novels about vile vacationsEvery summer, we long for a much-needed break from daily life, dreaming of self-reinvention in some distant paradise. entries.content:
Every summer, we long for a much-needed break from daily life, dreaming of self-reinvention in some distant paradise. But really, holidays can be absolute hell. Instead of relaxation we encounter heaving crowds, lumpy beds, the caprices of our loved ones and the grim truth that we can escape neither their worst failings nor our own, however far we travel.

Small wonder, then, that the disaster holiday has become a booming subgenre in fiction. For most of us, the levels of luxury promised by hit TV series The White Lotus are pure fantasy, yet we’re all vulnerable to the expensive promises we’ve been sold. Two of the smartest offerings in fiction this summer come from Claire Powell’s All In and Chloë Ashby’s Family Friends. In the former, a struggling couple whose marriage is on the rocks go on an all-inclusive Spanish weekend break, paid for by a rich brother. Poignant and extremely funny, the frictions that ensue are all too believable.

So, too, is the implosion of Ashby’s group of friends who have a decades-long custom of holidaying together in the south of France. This year, however, their marriages are threatened by one husband’s deceit, the lingering attraction between old friends and the arrival of a vivacious teenage stepdaughter. Poised and gripping, it uses a sweltering Mediterranean setting to amp up tensions to dramatic effect.

In Sabine Durrant’s superb thriller Dead Heat, meanwhile, a failed journalist, his more successful media friend and a former school contemporary, now a Gatsbyesque billionaire, find their Greek adventure transformed not only into a shameful reminder of racism in their shared past, but something outright murderous. Being thrown together to brave blazing summer heat only intensifies existing tensions as Durrant expertly brings the drama to a head.

Many characters seeking escape find that a change of scene only makes problems worse. Deborah Levy’s Hot Milk, adapted as a film last year by Rebecca Lenkiewicz, chronicles a family unravelling in a Spanish fishing village. Rose pays thousands to a clinic to cure her mysterious paralysis while Sofia distracts herself with local beauty, Ingrid, as unresolved conflicts between mother and daughter start to boil over.

A fateful holiday also inspires the scathing, semi-autobiographical play in Jo Hamya’s novel The Hypocrite. Sophia is taken out of school to act as her novelist father’s amanuensis, though he spends much of his time in Sicily seducing local women instead of bonding with his daughter. Years later, he is appalled to see that Sophia has adapted his parenting failures for the stage, though the novel cleverly hints at aspects of her own behaviour on that holiday which Sophia may have conveniently chosen to forget.

The fancier the surroundings, the worse a fictional holiday is likely to be. In William Rayfet Hunter’s Sunstruck, an invitation to his university friend Lily’s parents’ chateau is the catalyst for unwelcome epiphanies about the class and race differences between the narrator and Lily’s family, even as he becomes involved with her wayward brother. Lucy Foley’s The Midnight Feast also plays with this trope to great effect, when the opening weekend of a high-end wellness retreat in the West Country is disrupted by revelations from a guest’s disastrous stay many years before.

Our attempts to get away from it all can often lead us right back to what we left home to avoid. In Deepa Anappara’s ambitious, multilayered The Last of Earth, Victorian adventurer Katherine hopes her journey into the forbidden kingdom of Tibet will help her overcome difficult feelings about her heritage. Unfortunately, disguising herself as a male pilgrim to cross dangerous unknown terrain only serves to underline Katherine’s alienation as she attempts to become the first European woman to reach Lhasa.

In an unfamiliar setting, relaxed and away from our usual points of reference, we are more vulnerable to danger. Patricia Highsmith’s classic The Talented Mr Ripley posits the holiday abroad as a perfect space for murder and identity theft. In Sean Gilbert’s I’ll Be the Monster, a murderous husband and wife encounter an old university acquaintance while on a trip to Istanbul to revive their marriage. This unsettling novel disorients us by asking who is really the predator, and who is the prey.

The self-discovery that travel can bring is not always benign. Thirty years ago, Alex Garland’s cult bestseller The Beach lured in the reader with the promise of a mysterious idyll on a remote Thai island. However, the narrator’s true awakening is to how easily manipulated he and most of the other would-be lotus eaters really are. Painful self-awareness don’t come to a stop with parenthood, either. In Elena Ferrante’s The Lost Daughter, Leda allows a new acquaintance, downwardly mobile young mother Nina, to use her beach cottage for an illicit rendezvous. Even as Leda hypocritically judges Nina for struggling in the way that she once did, she is forced to come to terms with her own temporary abandonment of her daughters.

At once longed-for and disruptive, any break from place or routine can be double-edged. In my own debut novel, The Decadence, a group of former university friends break lockdown to holiday in a remote Devon country house during the pandemic. Too quarrelsome and intoxicated to notice that the house is in fact haunted, they do not realise they must band together against the danger until it is almost too late.

Despite all these fearsome warnings, venturing far from home can still bring vital insights. In EM Forster’s A Room With a View, Lucy Honeychurch scandalises her chaperone with the realisation that she must break off her engagement after being impulsively kissed by George Emerson in a field above Florence. David Nicholls’ bestselling You Are Here brings together lonely divorcees Marnie and Michael for a rainy hike across the Lake District, with love growing unexpectedly as they emerge from their self-protective shells.

We don’t always get exactly what we want from our holidays, but the adventure is in breaking away from the familiar. Even our most unpleasant travel experiences can be revelatory, and the best can transform us into new versions of ourselves, especially once they are safely behind us.

entries.title: I Give You My Silence by Mario Vargas Llosa review – Nobel laureate’s final novel is a love letter to Peru
entries.summary: This fascinating, eccentric book becomes a quirky primer on Peruvian music and cultureWhen I Give You My Silence was published in Spanish in 2023 its author, the Peruvian Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa, rightly predicted that it would be his final novel. entries.content:
When I Give You My Silence was published in Spanish in 2023 its author, the Peruvian Nobel laureate Mario Vargas Llosa, rightly predicted that it would be his final novel. He died last year at the age of 89. I Give You My Silence may have been completed with the spectre of death approaching, but there is nothing morbid about this book, which is an eccentric love letter to Vargas Llosa’s native country and, in particular, its music.

The novel’s quixotic hero is a music journalist called Toño Azpilcueta. Toño always hoped to be a professor of Peruvian music, but as the novel opens, he’s earning a meagre living teaching at a girls’ school and writing articles for specialist magazines. Luckily, he’s subsidised by his longsuffering wife, Matilde. Toño is a recognisable type: the impecunious cultural obsessive. If he were British, he would be fanatical about free jazz, or some obscure Delta bluesman. But this is Peru and Toño’s particular infatuation is the vals, a Peruvian musical style that fuses the European waltz with African and indigenous Latin American traditions.

One evening, Toño gets an invitation to see an unknown guitarist called Lalo Molfino, who blows him away with his incredible virtuosity. Before Toño has time to digest the musician’s brilliance, he learns of his sudden death. With the help of a small gift of money from a friend, Toño embarks on a project to write a biography of Molfino. “This book would be an homage to his talent, but also much more: he would at last put to paper those ideas about the Peruvian vals he had entertained so often.”

Toño’s Big Idea is that the vals is going to save Peru, and possibly humanity. Its blended heritage, he explains, points a way past the trauma that colonialism, racism, dictatorship and terrorism have inflicted on his country. Toño’s quest to write the book involves sleuthing, research, interviews, a journey along Peru’s Pacific coast to Molfino’s birthplace, and battles with his own demons – in particular, a phobia about rats.

Coming to this book with, I think, the median British knowledge of Peru (Machu Picchu, the Shining Path, ceviche, Paddington Bear), it took me a moment to orient myself. I knew nothing about the country’s music and I didn’t realise that Cecilia Barraza, an important recurring character, is a real-life Peruvian singer. (It’s a bit like having Patti Smith turn up in a novel.) Nor did I clock to begin with that the novel is really two books in one. The odd-numbered chapters are a third-person account of Toño’s attempt to research and write the biography. Most of the even-numbered chapters are excerpts from the final work, I Give You My Silence. These end up forming a quirky primer on Peruvian music and culture. It includes essays on the history of the vals; the lives of the musicians who created it; the cajon, a distinctive Peruvian percussion instrument; Spanish as a regional lingua franca; and huachafería, a concept that Toño sees as a key part of Peru’s identity. Huachafería holds huge significance for both Toño and Vargas Llosa. The novel’s translator, Adrian Nathan West, tells us in a helpful afterword that “dictionaries typically define it as pretension”. Toño is much more effusive: “Huachafería can be brilliant, but it is rarely intelligent: it is intuitive, verbose, solemn, melodic, imaginative and above all maudlin.”

This is, in fact, a perfect description of the book that Toño himself is writing, which includes the grandiose and impossible claim that “this book you hold in your hands, reader, will be the starting point of a true revolution that will pull our Peru up from poverty and sorrow, restoring its glory and its creativity, making it a place where all are truly equal and putting an end to the sad divisions of its people”.

Toño’s mission is clearly bonkers, but he approaches it with a heroic single-mindedness that wins the reader over. And the form the novel takes allows Vargas Llosa to have his cake and eat it too: giving Toño space to explore his ideas in detail, while simultaneously having fun pointing out how overheated they are.

For instance, one of Toño’s chapters tells the story of a love affair between Toni Lagarde and Lala Solórzano, a white man from a middle-class neighbourhood and a poor black woman from a rough one. Thanks to a shared interest in music, they meet, fall in love and get married. For Toño the polemicist, it’s proof of the redemptive power of the vals. But Toni and Lala reappear through the novel as he works on his book, gently pushing back at Toño’s efforts to make them emblematic of anything. “You’re the only ones who are free. And music opened your eyes. It made you two aware,” Toño tells them. “You’ve got a theory there, but there are lots of theories,” is Toni’s tactful answer. In another chapter, a psychiatrist who’s helping Toño deal with his rat phobia gives his book a much more savage assessment, calling it “a pointless, incoherent mass of undeveloped ideas”.

Vargas Llosa’s own implied verdict on Toño’s idiosyncratic attempt to save the world by writing a book about Peruvian music is more nuanced and tender. Vargas Llosa, of course, shared his central character’s idealism. At the time the novel takes place, in the early 1990s, Vargas Llosa was also on a failed mission to save Peru, running unsuccessfully to become his country’s president. And just as Toño sees something poignant and important in the maligned quality of huachafería, Vargas Llosa finds heroism in his unworldly protagonist.

Gentle, impractical dreamers like Toño, he seems to be saying, bring their own kind of changes into the world. One small proof of this is that by the novel’s end, I had followed Toño up the Pacific coast of Peru on Google Maps to the tiny settlement of Puerto Etén, tried to find a recipe for Lala’s quince marmalade online, made a vals playlist on Spotify and searched the prices of return flights to Lima. If I ever make it there, I’ll be sure to pack this fascinating and engaging book.

entries.title: You Won’t Get Free of It by Rachel Aviv review – a subtle study of the mother-daughter bond
entries.summary: The most complex of female relationships is thrown into sharp relief in this moving series of essaysRachel Aviv has a profound interest in the vagaries of human psychology: Strangers to Ourselves, her last book, profiled five people whose psychiatric states resisted straightforward explanation, testing the limits of the mental health system. A Pulitzer finalist, Aviv has become known for rigorous,
entries.content:
Rachel Aviv has a profound interest in the vagaries of human psychology: Strangers to Ourselves, her last book, profiled five people whose psychiatric states resisted straightforward explanation, testing the limits of the mental health system. A Pulitzer finalist, Aviv has become known for rigorous, penetrating journalism that is as empathic as it is insightful. Now comes You Won’t Get Free of It, six stories of mothers and daughters, all originally published in the New Yorker.

Madness runs through this book, too, in the stories of Linda Bishop, a woman who, upon discharge from hospital after a psychotic break, holed up in an abandoned farmhouse and tried to subsist on apples alone, and of Mary, a woman whose delusions and paranoia were only seemingly cured as a side-effect of chemotherapy. It’s also there in the childhood memories of the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus – a professional court witness for those who have been accused of abuse, one of whom was Harvey Weinstein. Loftus’s mother was found drowned, perhaps as a result of suicide. In Aviv’s masterly profile, she teases out a conclusion that leaves you pondering the extent to which this memory expert can rely on her own recollections, and what that says about her particular line of work.

Of the mother representing madness, Marguerite Duras said: “Our mothers always remain the strangest, craziest people we’ve ever met.” Yet there is psychological instability here on the part of daughters, too: Hannah Upp, whose story opens the collection, suffered from fugue states that would lead to her eventual disappearance. Aviv compassionately chronicles her mother’s desperate quest to find her.

In the preface, Aviv writes about her interest in the “hide and seek” dynamic of mother-daughter pairings, and indeed, each of these stories could be said to represent an acting out of that game. What is interesting is that Aviv, too, is a player. “It was as if I had failed to see the drama on the mother’s side, too – her particular longings and humiliations and needs,” she writes, of her own journalism.

Aviv admits to a previous “deficit of curiosity” about mothers. It is admirable how clear-eyed she is about these failures of imagination, which became apparent only after she herself became a mother. In Bishop’s case Aviv neglected to mention, or consider, the possible impact of a baby given up for adoption when Bishop was a young woman. “I had not even asked a follow-up question,” Aviv admits, and you can feel her embarrassment. She has gone back and remedied the “imbalance” for the purposes of this collection, but the discussion itself prompts a fascinating question: to what extent does a woman’s motherhood – or lack thereof – contribute to her perspective as a writer?

It is not a question with an easy answer, not least in the case of novelist Alice Munro. Aviv’s investigation into Munro’s utter failure to protect her daughter, Andrea, from the abuse of her partner, Gerry, is the standout piece here. While it is claimed Munro knew of the abuse, was able to make reference to it in her art (Aviv’s tracing of it through Munro’s writing is meticulous), she chose not to act. That choice – the cowardice of it – and its lifelong repercussions for her daughters may never have come fully to light were it not for the persistence of several journalists, Aviv included. Munro emerges a pathetic figure; I have been unable to read her since.

However our mothers behave, the fact is we will never truly know them. Aviv writes, not entirely comfortably, of how she is essentially living out her own mother’s dream career. The editorial comments she leaves on Aviv’s work – such as a note about caring for a suicidal friend on an article about mental illness – constitute for her daughter a “chronic delusion of reference”. It’s a neat theory – but as a writer whose mother sometimes gives similarly self-reflective feedback, I found myself wondering if what we have here is simply a mother’s insistence that she was, and remains, a person, if her daughter would only care to look.

entries.title: Barack Obama launches podcast about books that ‘shaped his worldview’
entries.summary: The former US president will host six episodes of A Great Book for Audible, discussing work from Toni Morrison and John le Carré to James BaldwinBarack Obama is set to host a podcast about books that have “profoundly shaped his worldview and our society”, from Song of Solomon by Toni Morrison to Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy by John le Carré.The podcast, called A Great Book with Barack Obama, will lau
entries.content:
Barack Obama is set to host a podcast about books that have “profoundly shaped his worldview and our society”, from Song of Solomon by Toni Morrison to Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy by John le Carré.

The podcast, called A Great Book with Barack Obama, will launch on Audible on 24 September.

In each of six episodes – produced by the Amazon-owned company in collaboration with the Obamas’s production company Higher Ground – the former US president will discuss one of his chosen titles with a guest.

Along with the Morrison and le Carré, Obama has chosen The Fire Next Time by James Baldwin, All the Pretty Horses by Cormac McCarthy, Gilead by Marilynne Robinson, and All the King’s Men by Robert Penn Warren.

“Great books have always helped me figure out who I am and what I believe,” said Obama. “The six books featured in this series have stayed with me throughout my life, and each one has something to teach us about the human experience.

“For this podcast, I invited some friends to explore why they resonate, how they can shape our understanding of ourselves and each other, and why literature matters now more than ever,” he said. “I hope listeners will be inspired to discover or rediscover books that change the way they see themselves and the world”. The podcast’s guests are yet to be announced.

Obama has publicly shared his favourite books for years, posting summer reading lists and end-of-year roundups. This summer’s list, which he published in late July, includes Kin by Tayari Jones, Vigil by George Saunders, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout, Transcription by Ben Lerner, and Cool Machine by Colson Whitehead.

While his roundups are often made up of recently published books, all of his picks for his podcast were published in the 20th century, except for Robinson’s Gilead, released in 2004. Robinson and Obama struck up a correspondence after he invited her to dinner at the White House, and in 2012, he awarded her the National Humanities Medal.

entries.title: Sinking ships, dark humour and really good bad guys: Beryl Bainbridge – ranked!
entries.summary: From the last days of the Titanic to desperate romantics, we rate the work of a British master of black comedyBainbridge’s novel of the last days on RMS Titanic was acclaimed and popular (“They probably thought it was the book of the film,” she said), and the scenes of the sinking are brilliantly delivered. “There is about me an element of showmanship,” says one character, but Bainbridge’s own sho
entries.content:
10 Every Man for Himself (1996)

Bainbridge’s novel of the last days on RMS Titanic was acclaimed and popular (“They probably thought it was the book of the film,” she said), and the scenes of the sinking are brilliantly delivered. “There is about me an element of showmanship,” says one character, but Bainbridge’s own showmanship is muffled here by her need to stick with facts, meaning the novel lacks the humour, fluidity and eccentricity of her others. And unlike her earlier books, the final tragedy never feels personal to the characters.

Sample line: “He did have layers, but like an onion they were all the same.”

9 Harriet Said … (1972)

Bainbridge’s darkest novel is about the teenage narrator and her older, cooler friend Harriet. “I’ve always run wild,” our girl says: a common trait in Bainbridge novels. (She herself was “expelled from school at the age of nine because of some dirty rhyme”.) When the narrator and Harriet get involved with a married man, there’s a lot of “adolescent trembling, swirls of nerves gone gold” – and mortal danger. It’s a story of power and corrupted innocence: but who’s corrupting whom?

Sample line: “It was nothing really. I hardly noticed. Just like going to the dentist. Not even as bad.”

8 Master Georgie (1998)

The fifth of Bainbridge’s novels to be shortlisted for the Booker prize – “our table was always the most cheerful, because we didn’t expect to win” – was another based on historical events. She turned to these after she “used up”her life in her earlier autobiographical novels. A subtle book that rewards rereading, it’s set around the Crimean war, narrated in turn by the hangers-on of medic George Hardy. The story comes as a series of snapshot moments, as the characters hurtle toward disaster. “One should never underestimate the disruptive force of haphazard actions,” says one, and Bainbridge’s characters know all about those.

Sample line: “Some people only weep inside, which I think wasteful.”

7 A Quiet Life (1976)

Of all Bainbridge’s novels, this offers the most direct account of her “terrifying” childhood in Liverpool when, as she later recalled, her mother and father fought so much “my brother and I would never be out of the house at the same time [so as] to stop them killing each other”. Through siblings Alan and Madge, we see their mother’s restless domestic rearrangements (“Everything in its place, though never for long”) and a bad-tempered father, but also the demons that drove him there. Little wonder that “Madge threw herself about in a transport of unexplained grief”. But it’s also a charming, funny, bittersweet portrait of a vanished world of meat pies, fruit drops and poultices on boils.

Sample line: “Though the war was over, Father was still caught in a cross-fire, harassed by battles, by phantom cities tumbling about his ears.”

6 Sweet William (1975)

Many of Bainbridge’s characters long for the transformative effects of love, are so hungry for change that they grab on to it, even if it’s not the right change. Playwright and lothario William provides it for as many women as will have him. (“What did you think when I first met you?” “I thought I had flu.”) Even as his deceits are uncovered, he gets away with it. “You don’t want to expect normality from him,” one of his lovers says to another. “He’s an artist after all.” The novel has the delicious shiver provided by a really good bad guy.

Sample line: “Her doctor said she was a healthy young woman – all normal. Not my heart, she thought. Surely my heart’s not normal.”

5 An Awfully Big Adventure (1989)

Set, like many of Bainbridge’s novels, in post-war Liverpool, this book brings us an ungovernable girl, Stella, and her efforts to become an actor. (Bainbridge acted before she wrote, and appeared in the eighth episode of Coronation Street in 1961.) She falls for the director, Meredith Potter, with his “Gestapo monocle”, as he prepares a production of Peter Pan. This is Bainbridge at her most demanding – “I don’t like to be obvious or spell things out” – and the reader must stay alert, but the rewards are rich.

Sample line: “[Meredith] had never known a father, being the issue of a man who smoked cigars and a girl plucked from the typing pool of the Cunard buildings in 1913.”

4 Injury Time (1977)

Bainbridge’s best books are both funny and sad: when, early on, her publisher suggested she write a black comedy, “it was like taking a cork out of a bottle”. This is an extreme example of the form: a farce, where everyone seems to be having an affair with everyone else, turns into a hostage drama as a dinner party is invaded by criminals. The darkest moments are rough even by Bainbridge’s standards, but the overall tone is exuberant, even antic.

Sample line: “Why couldn’t he pretend that he longed to leave his wife, so that she in return could pretend she wished he would?”

3 The Birthday Boys (1991)

Easily the best of Bainbridge’s novels based on historical events, this takes us into the minds of Robert Scott (“I’m simply no good when I’m not doing something”) and the four men who went with him to the South Pole – and part of the way back. “We did our business in our britches and shook the turds out when they froze.” Each voice is distinct and a brilliant act of ventriloquism from Bainbridge, but what underlies the men’s relationships as they crawl toward disaster is the great immovable glacier of the English class system.

Sample line: “How curious it is that passion has so little to do with feeling cheerful.”

2 The Bottle Factory Outing (1974)

Most of Bainbridge’s novels end in death: this one opens that way too. Mismatched friends Freda (who “longed to be flung into the midst of chaos”) and Brenda (who wears a coat in bed) both work at a bottling factory, where they navigate desires for and attention from their Italian colleagues. A works day out leads to chaos with horses, a broken toilet, a barrel of brandy, and more death. Here, slapstick and tragedy don’t alternate, but happen at the same time, as Bainbridge once more makes us laugh at things we shouldn’t be laughing at.

Sample line: “She supposed it was the fumes from the wine that kept them all in a constant state of lust.”

1 The Dressmaker (1973)

Desperate romantics are Bainbridge’s speciality. Sensible Nellie (“Never sit down on someone else’s lav and never eat a shop-bought meat pie”) isn’t one, but her sister Marge (“the big blaze that died down through lack of fuel”) is. So is the niece that lives with them, Rita, who falls in love with an American GI. This is Bainbridge at her best: shocking, sinister, and perfectly expressing her characters’ internal turmoil, which by some process of alchemy results in the blackest of comedy.

Sample line: “She wished she was Bette Davis, Joan Crawford, languidly sitting in a long dress, calling them darling, loving and loyal always – but cool like a snake, telling them to go before they told her.”

entries.title: John Berger: From Life by Tom Overton review – a vibrant biography of the pioneering critic
entries.summary: This multi-layered portrait is a fitting tribute to the man behind Ways of SeeingThe cultural critic John Berger was still alive and kicking when he donated his literary archive – heaped boxes of letters and notepads, sketches and scripts – to the British Library in 2009. entries.content:
The cultural critic John Berger was still alive and kicking when he donated his literary archive – heaped boxes of letters and notepads, sketches and scripts – to the British Library in 2009. From his home in the Alps, he proceeded to liaise with the collection’s curator, Tom Overton, sorting each item and recounting the wild stories behind them. When Overton sought permission to write Berger’s biography, though, the critic insisted that he wait a few years. Death changes the relationship between the writer and his subject. More often than not, it complicates and enriches it. Berger – who spent much of his career in passionate conversation with the past – probably knew that better than anyone.

Berger typically described himself as a storyteller, an elastic job title which allowed him to swing between fiction and poetry, essays and screenplays. Implicitly, too, the term helped frame his criticism as something propulsive and inclusive, an invitation to dance as opposed to a judgment from on high. Berger had no time for the “great man” theory of art as espoused by the popular historian Kenneth Clark and instead urged his audience to view each piece as a manifestation of society and politics: the tainted fruit of capitalism, inseparable from the marketplace. Oil paintings were status symbols. Nudes were the product of the lusty male gaze. Looking itself was a political act. “You cannot reply to me,” he would tell 1970s TV viewers, breaking the fourth wall to highlight the medium’s limitations. He liked pointing out the mechanics behind the manufacture of art, demystifying the process to better appreciate its results.

These days Berger’s reputation largely rests on Ways of Seeing, the insurrectionist 1972 BBC series which made him the critics’ equivalent of a rock star or cult leader. Enterprising viewers can still find him on YouTube. He’s the eloquent firebrand with a messianic gleam in his eye; the Marxist intellectual in open-necked patterned shirts. Overton, though, is at pains to stitch Ways of Seeing into its wider context – showing it as part of a continuum, one political project among many. His exuberant biography is thick with detail and lit by wonder. It strains to paint the whole canvas and give us the man in full, warts and all.

Raised in London, a child of the blitz, Berger suffered through boarding school and the army before a visit to a Picasso exhibition knocked the scales from his eyes and blew up his middle-class world. He enjoyed moderate success with his paintings and greater acclaim for his novels (one of which – the fractured, sporadically fabulous G – won the 1972 Booker prize). But he was at his most assured and compelling when using the art of others as a springboard to further, deeper inquiry. Berger regarded each work as a portal between time and space and was enthralled by the ways it could be lost and found in translation. Tellingly, his first broadcasting gig was with the BBC World Service, describing pictures in the National Gallery to listeners in west Africa.

“We never look at just one thing,” he said. “We are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves.” That’s certainly the case with John Berger: From Life. Overton is fascinated by Berger but also fascinated by his relationship with Berger and his approach is therefore unashamedly subjective, sliding from the familial third-person (always “John”, never “Berger”) to the direct address (“You”) and between the past and present tense (sometimes in the space of a single sentence). Like Berger in his TV studio, Overton points out the wires, referring to “the book you’re reading now” and “the old man who squats on my pages” and occasionally fretting that he’s left out important information. It’s an elaborate conceit, but it by and large works. There is no single version of a story, Berger argued. Each storyteller can’t help but bend the tale to their will.

Overton reveres Berger but he is frustrated by him, too. His life’s a hot mess; his very presence turns oppressive. He’s so authoritative on the page and so contradictory in the wild, a jumble of red-blooded Marxism and High Tory traditionalism. Berger writes elegantly and angrily about forced migration, mourning the loss of the old rural communities, but he lives as a self-imposed exile in Switzerland and France, splitting his time between different houses and women. Language, he concludes, is “potentially the only real human home”, but even this isn’t fixed; it can be breached at any time. By the end of his life, Overton notes, the man’s spoken English has taken on the grammatical patterns of French.

Berger’s health was already starting to fail when he donated his boxes to the British Library. Overton recalls their queasy close-quarter encounters in London and Paris: “Strong smell of leaky prostate, top-note of cigarettes and event wine.” Berger in the flesh is diminished, disappointing, “less present here than you are in the archive”, which is probably the case with most ageing artists. They’ve put the best of themselves on the canvas, page or screen. That’s where we’ll find them – in their work, in the past.

If there was a bright running thread through Berger’s portmanteau career, it was this preoccupation with the past and its connection to the present. The dead and the living are interdependent, he said. The stronger the link, the happier and healthier the society. Great paintings in a gallery allow us to travel in time. So too do some people, if they are skilled and sensitive enough. Berger’s 1967 book A Fortunate Man paid gorgeous tribute to Dr John Sassall, a country physician from the Forest of Dean whose work at times bordered on the supernatural. “The doctor,” Berger wrote, “is the familiar of death … the living intermediary between us and the multitudinous dead.” He might just as easily be talking about the role of great artists and critics. Possibly British Library curators as well.

“Do biographers always remake their subject in their own image?” Overton wonders as he sets about trying to transfer Berger to the page. Most likely they do, but that’s only half of the equation. The past whispers to the present; the dead and living coexist. Overton is a writer in part because of reading John Berger. The biographer’s prose style is his own but he writes in the same spirit – fired by curiosity and close-marking his subject; gesturing out to the reader as though to engage them in debate. His aim, he confesses, is to convince us that the critic is “sat across the page from me, reading every word, a part of the process,” and in fits and spurts he achieves just that.

Technically Berger’s no longer with us: he died in 2017 at the age of 90. But he’s still speaking on YouTube, still being reprinted and still provoking and inspiring a fresh generation of writers. That’s the kind of community and continuity that he always hungered for in his life; sweet karmic payback for a career in the arts. Switch sides, reset and keep the conversation flowing. Berger once spoke to the past from the present. Now, as if by magic, it is the other way around.
